newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr sits on highs, support solid.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr sits on highs, support solid.

text.p: The Australian dollar was content to sit on its mountain of gains at the midsession and gather its strength for the next leg of its meteoric uptrend.

Dealers said U.S. investment banks had been tempted to take profits around US$0.8115/20 this morning but the resulting pullback was confined to US$0.8098 -- impressivley shallow given the currency had risen over two cents so far this week.

Indeed, rumours of fresh samurai-linked demand soon had it back above 81 cents and traders reckoned those would-be buyers waiting for a deeper correction before getting aboard could well miss the bandwagon.

By 12.30 pm (0130 GMT) the dollar was settling in at US$0.8111/16, territory not visited since October 1990, having sprinted up to US$0.8080/85 late here Thursday from a lowly US$0.7962/67 the day before.

Traders said support looked solid beneath 81 cents and the immediate upward bias would last as long as US$0.8050 remained intact. Indeed, it would take a breach of US$0.7950 to turn the tide against the bulls now, they added.
Resistance had made an appearance at US$0.8120 but there was talk of hefty stop loss buy orders around US$0.8130 which could see the currency to US$0.8150 at least if triggered.
On the crosses the currency was up at 90.32/42 yen from 90.16/26 late Thursday and 88.65/64 the day before, and at 59.5 on its trade weighted index -- a five year high -- from 59.2.
Analysts noted that one interesting side effect of this strength was that it made another monetary easing by the Reserve Bank more likely.

"The rise in the dollar is a de-facto tightening of policy which it's hard to believe the RBA will welcome only a couple of weeks after it cut rates," said Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank. "It will also bear down on inflation, so another cut looks a little more likely for December."
That risk may give dollar bulls some pause, although the A$ yields would still be far above those in Japan even after a 0.5 point cut in official rates to 6.0 percent.

Supporters also pointed out that Canada had been cutting rates every month this year and its dollar had still risen steadily reflecting improved prospects for the economy next year and a favourable inflation performance.

Australian inflation had also fallen markedly and was set to remain under that in the U.S. for a year or more, which should also work to keep A$ assets attractive even if short term rates fall. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
